key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to call tools for the wrong reason—following superficial cues instead of actual task needs—especially after they become competent with the tool.
engineering_relevance: For robust agent systems, tool-use policies should be trained and audited for causality, because shortcut tool invocation can degrade reliability even when overall task accuracy looks strong.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue-tool correlations during RL training.
Tested counterfactual cases where cues remained but the tool was unnecessary to expose shortcut behavior.
Added a dense decision-level reward from an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was actually needed.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and the effect appeared only once the agent had already learned the target tool reliably.
watch_item: The mitigation depends on an LLM judge for tool-necessity feedback, which may introduce extra cost and its own judgment bias.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
